name: Lisbon
blurb: Home port. Merchants here pay well for anything from the south, and the crown rewards new charts.
kind: the deep anchorage of the Tagus

name: Porto
blurb: The granite city on the Douro. Cheap northern wine and English cloth; pays well for sugar and spices.
kind: a harbour behind the Douro bar

label: w
name: Lagos
blurb: Prince Henry's harbour on the Algarve. Wine and cloth are cheap here.
kind: a sheltered bay

label: s
name: Cádiz
blurb: Castile's island port, with the Seville trade behind it. Salt from the pans is cheap; gold and spices fetch the best prices on the coast.
kind: a deep bay

name: Sanlúcar
blurb: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Duke of Medina Sidonia's town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. Every ship for Seville crosses its bar. Wine and salt are cheap.
kind: a river mouth behind the bar of the Guadalquivir

name: Palos
blurb: Palos de la Frontera on the Río Tinto, a town of pilots and caravels that trades and raids down the African coast. Fish and wine are cheap.
kind: an estuary harbour on the Río Tinto

name: Seville
blurb: The greatest city of Andalusia, eighty kilometres up the Guadalquivir. Genoese bankers, Moorish cloth, oil and wine; it pays well for gold, sugar and dyes.
kind: a river port, eighty kilometres upstream

name: Ceuta
blurb: Portugal's fortress across the Strait since 1415. The garrison pays dearly for wheat, wine and cloth.
kind: a deep harbour under the fortress

name: Safi
blurb: A Moroccan port where Portuguese merchants buy wheat and the striped Moorish cloth the traders of Arguin want for their gold.
kind: an open roadstead off the beach

name: Funchal
blurb: Madeira. The new cane fields make sugar cheap.
kind: an open roadstead under the town

name: Lanzarote
blurb: A Canary outpost. Islanders gather orchil lichen for red dye.
kind: a harbour inside the reef

name: La Gomera
blurb: A Castilian island ruled by the Peraza lords from their stone tower. Dragon's blood, orchil and goats; the last water before the open sea.
kind: a deep volcanic bay

name: Santa Cruz
blurb: The new Castilian town on Tenerife, laid out where Lugo landed his army. Sugar cane is going in on the conquered land, and wine grapes on the slopes under the great mountain.
kind: an open roadstead under the mountains

name: Arguin
blurb: An island trading post in a shallow bay. Saharan gold reaches the coast here.
kind: an island behind the Arguin banks

name: Gambia River
blurb: Mandinka traders at the river mouth deal in ivory, pepper and gold.
kind: a river mouth with a bar

name: Serra Leoa
blurb: A great harbour under the Lion Mountains. The Temne trade ivory and pepper for cloth.
kind: a great natural harbour

name: Rio dos Cestos
blurb: The Grain Coast, named for the melegueta pepper its people sell cheaply by the basket.
kind: a river mouth with a shallow bar

name: Costa da Mina
blurb: The Gold Coast. Akan traders bring gold dust down from the forests and pay richly for cloth.
kind: a surf beach with the anchorage offshore

name: Cantor
blurb: A Mandinka market town far up the Gambia, where caravans from the gold country meet the river. Only a shallow ship can come this far.
kind: a river town, far upstream

name: Mpinda
blurb: The port of the Manikongo at the mouth of the great Zaire river. Copper, ivory and red tacula wood for cloth and wine.
kind: the deep mouth of the Zaire

name: São Tomé
blurb: A Portuguese island colony on the line. Its new sugar mills sell cheaply, and its traders deal in Benin pepper.
kind: a sheltered roadstead under the town

name: São Brás
blurb: A watering place in a bay beyond the Cape, where Dias found fresh water and Khoikhoi herders. Little trade, but the last good anchorage before the Indian Ocean.
kind: an open bay with a spring of fresh water

name: Porto Seguro
blurb: The safe harbour where Cabral came ashore in the Land of the Holy Cross. Brazilwood, the red dye wood, for the cutting.
kind: a river mouth behind the reef

label: w
name: Bruges
blurb: The great market of the north, reached through its outport of Sluis on the Zwin. Flemish cloth and German copper are cheap; sugar, dyes, wine and spices fetch the best prices this side of Italy. Portugal keeps a factory here.
kind: the silting channel of the Zwin at Sluis

name: Antwerp
blurb: A rising town up the deep Scheldt, with fairs twice a year. Copper and cloth are cheap; it pays well for sugar and spices, and better every year.
kind: a river port on the deep Scheldt

name: Bristol
blurb: England's western port on the Avon, where the tide runs higher than anywhere. Broadcloth and Iceland fish are cheap; it wants wine, salt and dyes. Its seamen whisper of islands far to the west.
kind: a tidal river harbour where ships take the ground at low water

name: Galway
blurb: A walled Irish town of merchant families at the mouth of the Corrib, trading fish and hides for the wine and salt of Iberia.
kind: a small harbour at the mouth of the Corrib

name: Valencia
blurb: The richest city of the Crown of Aragon. Its beach at the Grau ships wine and the sugar of Gandia; its bankers and silk merchants want gold, wheat and spices.
kind: an open beach at the Grau, with ships anchored off

name: Genoa
blurb: Home of the Salvago and the great Genoese houses: bankers to every crown in Europe. Spices come in from the Levant cheaper than anywhere in the west; gold, sugar and dyes fetch high prices.
kind: a deep harbour behind the mole

label: n
name: Marseille
blurb: The French king's port on the Mediterranean since 1481, its galleys and its Levant trade behind the chain across the Old Port. Salt from the Camargue is cheap; French cloth and Provençal wine go out.
kind: the Old Port, behind its chain

label: n
name: Naples
blurb: The greatest city in Italy, capital of a kingdom ruled by a branch of the house of Aragon, on its bay under Vesuvius. Greco wine is cheap; everything else is bought, and dear.
kind: a broad bay under Vesuvius

label: e
name: Palermo
blurb: The capital of Sicily, the King of Aragon's granary: wheat is cheaper here than anywhere in the Mediterranean, and Sicilian sugar and Trapani salt go out with it.
kind: the Cala, inside the mole

name: Salé
blurb: A Moroccan port behind a dangerous bar at the mouth of the Bou Regreg. Wheat and Moorish cloth are cheap, and nobody asks where a cargo came from.
kind: a river mouth behind a dangerous bar

name: Algiers
blurb: A Berber town on the Barbary coast, its anchorage sheltered by a chain of islets. Wheat and Moorish cloth, and corsairs' plunder sold quietly.
kind: an anchorage sheltered by a chain of islets

name: Angra
blurb: A new Portuguese settlement on Terceira in the Azores, under the green bulk of Monte Brasil. Wheat and woad are cheap; the settlers want everything else.
kind: a sheltered bay under Monte Brasil

name: Flores
blurb: The westernmost of the Azores, all cliffs and waterfalls, with nobody on it. Orchil grows on the rocks; a house could settle it.
kind: an open cove under the cliffs

name: Ribeira Grande
blurb: A green valley on Santiago in the Cape Verde islands, with water and palms in a dry land. Salt is cheap from the pans of the islands; ships for Guinea call for water and food.
kind: an open roadstead at the mouth of a valley

name: St John's
blurb: A deep harbour behind narrows in the New Found Land, on the edge of the richest fishing banks in the world. Cod for the taking; salt and everything else must be brought.
kind: a deep harbour behind narrows

name: Santo Domingo
blurb: The mouth of the Ozama on the island the Taíno call Ayiti. Its caciques trade river gold and red dyewood for cloth, copper and brass.
kind: the mouth of the Ozama river

name: Calicut
blurb: The pepper port of the Malabar coast, ruled by the Zamorin, months of sailing beyond the Cape. Pepper, cinnamon and cloves, for gold, copper and fine cloth.
kind: an open roadstead off the Malabar coast

name: A hidden cove
blurb: A narrow bay on the empty east coast of Fuerteventura, out of sight of any lookout. Smugglers and corsairs water here, and nobody asks where a cargo came from.
kind: a narrow bay behind a reef
